en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Similes,
Section on the Donkey.
10. The Question on the Monkey’s Limbs “Venerable Nāgasena, when you say, ‘Two limbs of a monkey should be adopted,’ which are those two limbs that should be adopted?

“Just as, O King, a monkey, when seeking a place to dwell, takes up residence in such a spot as a vast, secluded great tree with branches on all sides—a place of refuge for the timid—so too, O King, should a monk seek out a dwelling.”
In the same way, great king, a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, [should rely] upon such a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta):
one who is modest, refined, virtuous, of noble character, learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, a bearer of the Vinaya, dear, worthy of honor, one who speaks, patient in speech,
an advisor, an instructor, one who shows the way, one who encourages, one who inspires, and one who gladdens.
"One should dwell depending upon a teacher.
This, Great King, is the first quality of the monkey that should be adopted.
Furthermore, Great King, the monkey moves, stands, and sits only in the tree; if it falls asleep, it spends the night right there."

In the same way, Great King, a practitioner of yoga should face toward the forest; he should stand, walk, sit, lie down, and fall asleep only in the forest, and there itself he should experience the foundations of mindfulness.
This, Great King, is the second quality of the monkey that should be adopted.
And this, Great King, was said by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma:
Whether walking, standing,
sitting, or lying down,
the bhikkhu shines in the forest.
"...is described as being like the end of the wind.
The tenth question, on the monkey's horn.
The first chapter, on the donkey.
Its summary verse (uddāna) is:
The donkey and the cock,
the crow, the hyena, and the leopard.
The elephant, the bamboo, the bow,
the crow, and then the monkey.
